analysis.one_liner: Spends over $435 billion on child care, health, jobs, housing, and water, and raises the minimum wage to $15.
analysis.headline: Introduced by 26 senators in the final two weeks of the 116th Congress, the $435 billion Economic Justice Act died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have spent more than $435 billion responding to the economic damage COVID-19 inflicted on low-income and minority communities [S3]. It funded child care stabilization, community health centers and hospitals, job training, small-business lending, broadband, school and water infrastructure, and affordable housing [S2][S3]. It also raised the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour, restored a higher overtime salary threshold, pushed holdout states to expand Medicaid with a richer federal match, and created a down-payment tax credit for first-time homebuyers and a renters credit [S2][S3]. Introduced on December 18, 2020, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and received no further action before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would gain from a $15 minimum wage and restored overtime pay; low-income and minority communities would gain from child care stabilization, community health center and hospital funding, maternal health programs, job training, and anti-poverty formula funds; renters and first-time homebuyers would get new tax credits; rural, tribal, and low-income communities would get water, broadband, and school construction money [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a child care stabilization grant program with $50 billion appropriated, requiring providers to keep paying full staff wages, cap family copayments, and prioritize essential workers' children and low-income families [S3].

Appropriates $7.6 billion for community health centers, $2 billion for their capital projects, $750 million for hospital infrastructure, and $2.5 billion for the National Health Service Corps, targeting underserved areas [S3].
Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour and restores a higher salary threshold for overtime under the Raise the Wage Act and Restoring Overtime Pay Act subtitles [S2][S3].
Offers an increased federal Medicaid match to states that cover newly eligible individuals, a down-payment tax credit for first-time homebuyers, and a renters tax credit [S2][S3].

Funds broadband access including tribal broadband and device programs, drinking-water and clean-water projects for small and disadvantaged communities, and school, library, and minority-serving-institution construction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The $435 billion is designated as emergency spending with no revenue offsets in the bill, so the cost falls on federal borrowing and future taxpayers [S3]. Employers of low-wage workers would bear the cost of the $15 minimum wage and the higher overtime salary threshold [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The full $435 billion is designated as an emergency requirement under pay-as-you-go rules, meaning it adds to the deficit with no paying-for provisions in the introduced text [S3].

The phased $15 minimum wage and higher overtime threshold raise labor costs, and the strongest good-faith objection is their effect on small employers with thin margins, particularly in lower-wage regions [S2][S3].

The bill routes money through state lead agencies and dozens of existing grant programs with detailed application, reporting, and verification requirements, which could slow disbursement to families and providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed needs that were acute at the time — collapsing child care providers, strained community health centers, and the wage floor frozen at $7.25 — and its costs were real but conventional for emergency legislation: deficit spending and higher labor costs for some employers. Its biggest flaw was timing and process: introduced two weeks before the Congress ended, it never received a committee markup where design questions like the deficit cost or the minimum-wage phase-in could be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 18, 2020, two weeks before the Congress ended, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and died there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the bill with 25 cosponsors (24 Democrats and 1 Independent) on December 18, 2020 [S1][S4].

The bill proposed more than $435 billion in investments in child care, health care, workforce training, small business, broadband, housing, and water infrastructure, plus a $15 minimum wage and Medicaid expansion incentives [S3][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the last action of any kind recorded [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee, unscheduled and unvoted [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one received the funding the bill promised. Low-wage employers were spared the $15 minimum wage and higher overtime threshold, and the $435 billion in emergency spending never occurred, while the child care, health, and housing needs the bill targeted went unaddressed by this legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers and inactive committee leaders

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the $435 billion Economic Justice Act in the final weeks of the 116th Congress.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors (24) and the chamber's Independent
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, including Senators Murray, Wyden, Durbin, Brown, Booker, Harris, Sanders, and Klobuchar.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee; it received no committee action.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor in the lame-duck session and never brought the bill up for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Senate took no action after the referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: A $50 billion stabilization fund would pay providers' payroll, rent, and sanitation costs while requiring them to hold families harmless from copays and keep staff at full wages [S3].

The $15 minimum wage and a higher overtime salary threshold would raise their labor costs; their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the wage gains workers would have received [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Community health centers, hospitals, and health workforce programs
industries.note: Billions in new grants for health centers, hospital construction, nursing and medical school expansion, and loan repayment, concentrated in underserved areas [S3].
A broadband connectivity fund, tribal broadband set-asides, and E-rate device support would send federal money toward expanded service to unconnected households [S3].
Emergency support, bond guarantee reform, and new lending programs would channel federal capital through community lenders to small businesses in communities of color [S3].
Grants for water systems, school and library construction, and hospital projects, with Buy American iron and steel requirements, would generate construction work [S3].
A richer federal match to incentivize expansion would add newly covered members in holdout states, delivered through private Medicaid plans as well as public channels [S2][S3].
